versions.text:
For many summers Tamsin Rowe has led a July walk through the Hatherby cutting, where a railway once ran between an old platform and a brick footbridge. Volunteers with red torches walk it in about 42 minutes, marking each green light on a map. Every light is a wingless female glow-worm. What she needs is a tall grass stem to climb after full dark, where she glows to draw flying males; her larvae live in the turf and feed on snails. Rowe's first walk found 35, and the usual total is now about ninety.

That spring the Hatherby Line Trust made several changes to the cutting. In March it put up 23 solar lamps at the platform end. In April it widened the path and laid gravel along it. In May its contractor did the mowing of the banks, usually left until September. And because the trust now locks the platform gate at ten, the walk was moved an hour earlier, to half past nine.

Last July the count fell to 16. The trust's first step was to have the gravel raked back from the foot of each bank and the bare strip returfed.

It had been a dry spring, and the dry weather held into June, so Rowe laid 28 snail boards along the banks. They came up crowded. She then repeated the walk at the old hour of half past ten and found much the same low total. On the maps, a steep strip below the footbridge, beyond reach of the mowing, looked just like the mown banks beside it. Every missing light lay at the platform end, within reach of the lamps; past the last lamp the banks shone as thickly as ever, right down to the new gravel.

The trust has switched the lamps off for June and July. But the field behind the platform has since been sold, and plans for sixty houses show street lights along its edge, a few yards from the bank where the females climb. The planning hearing is in March.

The contractor, Joss Hebden, came to the next walk himself, on his knees at the steep strip with a red torch like everyone else. He has moved the mowing back to September, paid to reseed the bare banks out of his own pocket, and asked Rowe for a copy of her map, which he now keeps in his van.

For many summers Tamsin Rowe has led a July walk through the Hatherby cutting, where a railway once ran between an old platform and a brick footbridge. Rowe's first walk found 16, and the usual total is now about ninety. Last July the count fell to 28.

The walk follows the same pattern each year. On a still night, volunteers with red torches set out from the platform and take about 23 minutes to reach the footbridge, marking each green light on a map. Since the trust began locking the platform gate at ten, they have started an hour earlier, at half past nine.

Every light is a wingless female glow-worm. What she needs is a tall grass stem to climb after full dark, where she glows to draw flying males; her larvae live in the turf and feed on snails. That spring the cutting had changed: the Hatherby Line Trust put up 35 solar lamps at the platform end, widened the path with gravel, and had its contractor do the mowing of the banks in May rather than September. The trust's first step after the low count was to switch the lamps off for the rest of the summer.

In August the trust held a meeting in the village hall, and Rowe brought her maps. Her own walk at the old hour of half past ten had found much the same low total. The losses were spread evenly: under the lamps and past them, on the mown banks and on the steep strip below the footbridge beyond reach of the mowing, along the new gravel and on the far bank well away from it. One record followed them. After a dry spring, her 42 snail boards had come up nearly bare, and where snails were scarcest the lights were scarcest too.

Rowe had bought the boards herself after the trust's committee voted against paying for them. The committee has since told its members that the weather was to blame and that switching the lamps off was a sensible precaution. The boards, and the six weeks of mornings the volunteers spent lifting them, get no mention.

Because the trust now locks the platform gate at ten, the walk had also moved an hour earlier, to half past nine.

Even after the dry spring, the boards came up crowded. On the maps, the losses were spread evenly: under the lamps and past them, on the mown banks and on the steep strip below the footbridge beyond reach of the mowing, along the new gravel and on the far bank well away from it. At half past nine in July the sky is still pale. So the gate was left open one night, and a volunteer held the footbridge rail and watched the banks below light up one by one; the walk at the old hour of half past ten counted close to the usual ninety.

The trust will open the gate for the walk each July; on every other night it stays locked at ten. For years villagers walked the cutting after dark, children on their parents' shoulders counting lights to the footbridge, and Rowe's oldest maps carry their pencilled tallies, in hands she can still name.

Rowe's first walk found 28, and in recent summers the usual total has been about ninety. Last July the count fell to 42.

It had been a dry spring, and the cutting had changed. In March the Hatherby Line Trust put up 16 solar lamps at the platform end; in April it widened the path with gravel, so that more visitors could come and see the glow-worms; in May its contractor did the mowing of the banks, usually left until September. Because the trust now locks the platform gate at ten, the walk had also moved an hour earlier, to half past nine. The trust's first step after the low count was to stop all mowing of the banks until September.

Rowe held that the maps would settle more than any guess. Her 23 snail boards, laid after the dry spring, came up crowded, and her walk at the old hour of half past ten found much the same low total. Under the lamps the banks had lost about as many lights as the dark stretch beyond them, and the steep strip below the footbridge, beyond reach of the mowing, had lost as many as the mown banks. The losses ran in two thin lines along the path, where the turf the females grew up in had lain under the gravel since April.

That autumn the trust lifted a foot of gravel from each side of the path and sowed grass. The sign it put up at the platform gate that spring is still there, inviting visitors to take the wider path and see the glow-worms of Hatherby. Rowe has asked the trust to keep it.
